summary: This experimental document describes a way to detect whether end-to-end data flows share a common bottleneck. It computes summary statistics from continuous measurements and feeds them to a grouping algorithm that runs wherever the knowledge is needed. It supports coupled congestion control for RTP media.

eli5.summary: If two cars are stuck at the same narrow bridge, they can notice that together. This is a way for traffic streams to figure out they are in the same jam.

questions: how to detect a shared bottleneck
how do rtp flows know they share a congested link
what is skewness in network metrics
how does coupled congestion control work
subtitle: Detecting when multiple RTP media flows compete for the same bottleneck link.

tldr.problem: When RTP media flows share a bottleneck link, they need to detect this shared congestion so coupled congestion controllers can coordinate their sending rates and avoid unnecessary packet loss and delay.
tldr.mechanism: The algorithm measures one-way delay and packet loss on each flow, calculates summary statistics that capture the shape of the delay distribution (skewness, variability, oscillation), and groups flows that show similar statistical characteristics.
tldr.outcome: Flows that share a bottleneck can be grouped together and have their congestion control coordinated, improving the efficiency of multi-party communication applications.

today: RFC 8382 is an Experimental specification published in June 2018. It has not been obsoleted or updated by later RFCs and remains the primary specification for measurement-based shared bottleneck detection for coupled congestion control.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
In interactive RTP media applications like multi-party video, a single sender often communicates simultaneously with multiple peers, creating multiple data flows. These flows may or may not traverse the same bottleneck links on the Internet. When multiple flows share a bottleneck, they compete for bandwidth and can cause each other to experience increased packet loss and delays.

RFC 8382 describes a measurement-based approach to detect when flows share a common bottleneck. This detection is essential for coupled congestion control schemes, which coordinate the sending rates of multiple flows to honor their priorities and reduce unnecessary packet loss and delay. The mechanism groups flows with similar statistical characteristics and relies on continuous measurements of packet delay and loss.
sections.eli5: When you're sending video to multiple people and they're all on the same slow connection, you need to notice that and adjust how fast you send. This is the method to figure out when streams are stuck together.

sections.title: Measurement Signals and Key Terms
sections.content:
The detection mechanism uses two primary signals: packet loss and one-way delay (OWD). Packet loss indicates congestion but is relatively infrequent and noisy on its own. One-way delay—the time a packet takes to travel from sender to receiver—is a cleaner signal, though it includes delays from every device on the path, not just the bottleneck.

The algorithm avoids the problem of absolute delay by working with relative one-way delay measurements. Because senders and receiver clocks may not be synchronized, the mechanism computes statistics relative to the mean OWD rather than absolute values. This approach is sufficient because sender and receiver clock skew typically remains constant over the measurement periods used by the algorithm, allowing the offset to be subtracted out mathematically.
sections.eli5: The algorithm measures how long packets take to arrive and whether any get lost. It doesn't need perfectly synchronized clocks—just the differences between delays matter.

sections.title: Summary Statistics and Flow Metrics
sections.content:
The core of the mechanism is computing four summary statistics over a measurement interval. These statistics describe the shape of the delay distribution and work together to discriminate flows that share a bottleneck:

Skewness estimate measures whether delays cluster below or above the mean. Variability estimate (Mean Absolute Deviation) captures the spread of delays. Oscillation estimate counts significant crossings of the mean delay, indicating low-frequency fluctuations. Packet loss serves as a supplementary measure—when loss becomes high, it becomes a reliable indicator of congestion.

These statistics are calculated incrementally over a base time interval T, with parameters controlling the measurement window. Recommended values from practical testing are T=350 milliseconds and N=50, using parameters like skewness threshold c_s=0.1 and oscillation threshold p_f=0.1.
sections.eli5: The algorithm calculates four numbers about each stream: how skewed the delays are, how spread out they are, whether they oscillate, and how many packets are lost. Streams with similar numbers are probably stuck together.

sections.title: Flow Grouping Algorithm
sections.content:
The grouping algorithm works in stages. First, it identifies which flows are actually experiencing a bottleneck (as opposed to just seeing normal path variation) using the skewness estimate and packet loss. Then it progressively divides flows into groups based on the four statistics.

The process sorts flows by oscillation estimate and groups those with similar values. It then subdivides each group by variability, then by skewness, and finally by packet loss (when packet loss is high enough to be reliable). This sorting-based approach is simple, efficient for 10 to 20 flows, and uses threshold parameters (p_f, p_mad, p_s, p_d) to decide when flows are similar enough to group.

The algorithm achieves full accuracy only after collecting measurements over 2*M time intervals, and it includes hysteresis to avoid constantly switching group membership as network conditions fluctuate.
sections.eli5: The grouping algorithm sorts streams by how similar their delay patterns are and puts streams with matching patterns into the same group. A group means these streams share a bottleneck.

sections.title: Deployment Scenarios
sections.content:
The mechanism can be deployed in three ways. Sender-based: senders calculate all statistics from feedback data, determining shared bottlenecks locally. This is recommended when using sender-based congestion control. Receiver-based: receivers measure one-way delay and packet loss, compute summary statistics, and send them to senders, which perform grouping. This reduces feedback overhead. Cooperative: receivers compute and share statistics, while both senders and receivers can perform grouping determinations, enabling more advanced shared bottleneck detection.

The RFC also describes enhancements for improving responsiveness under changing conditions (weighting recent measurements more heavily) and removing noise from non-bottleneck paths. Security considerations note that unauthenticated RTCP packets carrying delay measurements or shared bottleneck indications could allow attackers to alter congestion characteristics; the security of the transport protocol and coupled congestion controller apply.
sections.eli5: The measurement can happen at senders, receivers, or both, depending on what's convenient. An important reminder: an attacker could mess with the measurement data, so use secure RTP versions.
